title: Designing Destructive Actions
summary: This lesson explores six UI patterns to handle destructive actions like deletion safely. It teaches how to use friction, specific labeling, and visual hierarchy to prevent accidental user errors.

transcript.text: Hold to delete. Release early, nothing dies.
The ring is the confirmation. 300 milliseconds of commitment replace a dialog. Release early and the action never fires.
Pattern 02 - Labels. Name the action. 'Are you sure?' 'Yes.' Nobody reads that. Name the action: 'Delete project', 'Keep project'. The verb is the warning.
Pattern 03 - Placement. Off the happy path. Destructive buttons never sit where confirm lives. Muscle memory clicks primary spots blind. Move delete away and autopilot can't reach it.
Pattern 04 - The Red Budget. Red is a budget. Spend it on destruction only. A red logout button cries wolf, then delete looks routine.
Pattern 05 - Danger Zone. Bury it at the bottom. GitHub buries deletion in a danger zone. Bordered, labeled, last position on the page. Geography is friction.
Pattern 06 - Cooldown. The last line of defense. Some platforms add a cooldown. Deletion scheduled. 14 days to change your mind. Time is the last line of defense.
Destructive actions are a design language. Follow for more UX engineering. Save this before you ship a delete button.

DESTRUCTIVE ACTIONS. Danger is a design language.
design_principles: Use specific verbs in labels instead of generic 'Yes/No'
Avoid muscle memory errors by moving destructive buttons away from primary spots
Red budget: reserve red color exclusively for destruction
Geography is friction: bury dangerous actions at the bottom
Cooldown periods as a last line of defense
before_after: Transforming generic confirmation dialogs and poorly placed delete buttons into intentional, friction-based interactions like hold-to-confirm and danger zones.
